k-1.x_notes: Strengths: nine problems that build real backward-induction ideas using the child-friendly word 'trap' from the outline. The problems go from an immediate win, to 3 being a trap, to classifying 1-12 (traps 3, 6, 9, 12), to a reply tree from 6 (P4) that shows 'answer every reply' concretely, to finding the one bad move in an 8-counter game record (row 3, a unique answer that I checked), choosing who goes first with 9, finding traps above 12 and 20, the {1,2,3} rule (traps 4, 8, 12), and two piles that include the non-obvious second-player win at (4,1). All answers check out, the boxes are large, and the band will not run out of work. Weaknesses: there is a Name field in every header and no proper footer. P1 and P2 are tiny one-step questions that break the start into directed steps. P5 asks a kindergartner to read a game record, which is a lot. The rules box and the definition box add some reading.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: header and footer follow the format, there is no Name field, and the shared rule is stated once in short sentences. There are plenty of concrete actions on the page: color stars for winning piles 1-6, cross out the right counters for piles 4-11 (all correct), circle the losing piles 1-15 on dot towers, play a grown-up with 20, the {1,2,3} rule for piles 3-8, the {1,3} parity rule for piles 1-9, and two rows that include the non-mirror case (2,3). All answers check out and there is a good variety of rules. Weaknesses: the marking switches between star = you win, circle = partner wins, and 1st/2nd, which could confuse K children. P1 and P3 cover nearly the same question. 'Color a star each time you win' is a little reward-chart-like. Three of the four two-row cases are plain mirror positions. There is less work on answering every reply or finding mistakes.
k-1.reason: Both are correct and will keep the band busy, and Y is cleaner on format. X develops the K-1 idea further, with the reply tree, the mistake-spotting, large traps and a non-obvious two-pile case, so it answers the 'too dumbed down' complaint better. X's small opening steps and Name field are quick to fix.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: closely aligned to the 2-3 emphasis. It goes straight to {1,3,4}, starting concretely with playing from 6, then a 1-20 W/L table (L = 2, 7, 9, 14, 16), two claims to test (greedy 'take 4' and copying the opponent from 8, both false), a 16-counter game record with exactly two mistaken turns (2 and 3, which I verified), a winning plan for 14 that must answer every move, extension to 23/28/33/50/100, the {1,3,5} rule to describe for all piles, and two {1,3,4} piles (all five answers check out, including (6,4) as a second-player win). Real backward induction throughout, with roomy workspace. Weaknesses: Name field and non-standard footer. P3 and P4 only ask 'Is the claim correct?' and may get one-word answers. The two-pile {1,3,4} problem is very hard for third graders. The rule box is a little formal.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: format follows the standard. A {1,2} table to 20 and big piles (24/29/31/45 with the first move), then a {1,3,4} table, five well-chosen claims (Mia/Leo/Zoe/Sam/Ana, all with correct verdicts, including the greedy fallacy), extension to 30/50/100, two rows with {1,2} including the non-obvious (3,6) and (1,4) second-player wins, and four rules compared at 35 (first, first, second, second; I checked each). Weaknesses: the first two problems repeat the {1,2} game, which is the K-1 content and below this band's emphasis. P7 asks for four answers with no tables or explanation space, so it is hard to support. 'Explain' is appended in several places. There is no game-record or full-plan task, so backward induction against every reply gets less direct attention.
grades-2-3.reason: Both are mathematically sound and substantial. X spends the hour on the band's target ({1,3,4}, testing claims against every reply, analyzing a game record, building a full plan), while Y spends its first third on the easier {1,2} game. X's format fixes are trivial.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: very rich and correct mathematics with concise, substantial problems: prove the {1,2} pattern; label {1,3,4} piles 0-29 and prove the pattern; the greedy player wins only from 1, 3, 4, 6 and 11 (a surprising finite answer, which I verified); find every move set with the same losing piles as {1,3,5} (all sets of odd numbers containing 1); {1,2,m}, which keeps multiples of 3 unless 3 divides m, otherwise period m+1; the {1,6,9} table to 39, with repetition starting at 10 and period 5, both visible on the page (I checked); the pigeonhole proof of eventual periodicity; Grundy values for {1,3,4} (period-7 pattern 0,1,0,1,2,3,2); and two-pile positions (6,4) and (12,5) lose, (5,1) and (11,3) win, all correct. Covers all three kernels. Weaknesses: abstract for fourth graders (set notation, parameter m, 'every finite set', a mex definition) and little concrete play at the start. A second rule box appears mid-packet. Name field. P10 states the result it asks children to prove.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: clean format and a concrete, table-driven sequence: {1,2} and {1,2,3} to 20; 100 counters under each rule with an exact strategy; {1,3,4} to 30; 100 and 1000 with why the pattern persists; {1,3,5}, {1,4} and {1,4,5} compared; {1,2,m} for m = 4-7 (only 6 changes it, which I checked); inverse design problems (5,10,15 by {1,2,3,4}; 4,8,12 with 5 by {1,2,3,5}; evens with 2 impossible; only-3, which hinges on finite vs infinite lists and makes a good discussion); and two-pile grids for {1,2} and {1,3,4}, a strong visual discovery task. Weaknesses: a lot of mechanical labeling (seven rules times 24 piles, plus 70 more table cells) risks feeling like routine practice. The opening {1,2}/{1,2,3} work is easy for this band. 'Explain' is appended to many problems. No eventually-periodic example with an irregular start, no general periodicity argument, and greed is not addressed.
grades-4-5.reason: Y is more concrete and easier to start, but much of it is repeated table-filling. X's problems are deeper and better chosen (greedy fails, the irregular start of {1,6,9}, the pigeonhole proof, {1,2,m}), and with a mathematician at the table they give 40 minutes of real investigation.

overall.reason: Both packets are mathematically correct throughout and would keep every band busy. Y follows the page format better and is a bit more concrete. X develops the ideas more deeply and more on-target in every band: reply trees and game-record mistakes for the younger bands, and greedy, irregular-start periodicity and pigeonhole for 4-5. Its main defects (Name fields, footers, a few tiny opening steps) are quick to edit.
